processing: Bred for shading: usually covered before picking and made into tencha for matcha, and also used for gyokuro; a few makers roast it into houjicha.
harvest_season: Spring first flush, shaded before picking, as is usual for matcha and gyokuro cultivars.
appearance_dry: As matcha, a fine powder whose strong green colour is one of the cultivar's selling points.
appearance_wet: Whisked matcha leaves no whole leaf; shaded tencha or gyokuro leaf is soft and deep green.
taste_profile: High in umami with low astringency, and a sweet, slightly creamy aroma.

brewing.notes: Sift and whisk as for any good matcha. Its low astringency makes it forgiving, and it holds up well in a thicker bowl.

vintage_note: Sold by cultivar and maker, normally from the latest spring harvest and without a vintage year on the label. It is still uncommon, since it was announced only in 2017, so most offers are small single-cultivar lots.
description:
Seimei is a modern Japanese cultivar bred with matcha in mind. Compared with Yabukita it is reported to have better colour and flavour and, when shaded, a higher yield.

It takes well to covering, which is why most of it ends up as tencha and then matcha, sometimes as gyokuro. A few producers go the other way and roast it as houjicha.

The cup is rich in umami and low in astringency, with a sweet, faintly creamy aroma. Brew it like any quality matcha: sifted powder, water well below boiling, a quick whisk.

It is still a rare name on the shelf, and you are more likely to meet it blended unnamed than as a single cultivar. When you do find it alone, try it against Saemidori, one of its parents, to see what the breeding changed.
history:
Seimei was bred at NARO's Institute of Fruit Tree and Tea Science in Makurazaki, Kagoshima, from a 1992 cross of Fuushun and Saemidori, and registered in 2017.

It is reported to resist cold well and can be grown as far north as Saitama Prefecture.
